summary: Deep technical session focused on networking design for private VPC deployment of Redwood runtime. Covered PrivateLink vs. NLB, NAT/Gateway tradeoffs, subnet sizing, DNS and split-horizon, and runtime implications for latency/throughput (KV cache, batching, quantization). Agreed next steps to share diagrams, run a staging latency benchmark, and schedule KMS discussion.
topics: Runtime performance: KV cache, batching, quantization
transcript:
[00:00:00] Lena (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:00:06] Priya (Aurelius): Priya here, CTO, Marcus and Sofia from infra are on.
[00:00:12] Marcus: Marcus, Ops.
[00:00:15] Sofia: Sofia, network.
[00:00:18] Diego (Redwood): Diego here, solutions engineer, I'll run the deep-dive.
[00:00:22] Lena: Great. Goal for today is to walk through private VPC networking for the Redwood runtime and talk performance implications for latency and throughput. Approx 60 minutes, then next steps.
[00:00:37] Priya: Sounds good. We are particularly worried about latency for synchronous calls from our product where 95th percentile matters. Also need any details for our security/compliance folks.
[00:00:48] Diego: Totally. We'll cover PrivateLink, NLB, NAT egress, DNS, and then how runtime knobs like KV cache and batching interact with network topology.
[00:00:56] Sofia: Quick note - our VPC has a 10.0.0.0/16 CIDR, split across three AZs, currently using NAT gateways in two public subnets and some peering to analytics VPC.
[00:01:08] Diego: Perfect, that helps.
[00:01:12] -- Presentation share (link to deck) --
[00:01:20] Diego: First, PrivateLink model: we expose an endpoint service in our account, you create interface endpoints in your VPC, traffic stays on AWS backbone, no public IPs required. Pro: no internet egress, better security posture. Con: extra ENIs per AZ and cross-AZ traffic if endpoints are not co-located.
[00:01:45] Marcus: For high throughput, are ENI counts a limit? We have thousands of pods but only a handful of clients hitting inference.
[00:01:53] Diego: ENIs are per-subnet and instance limits matter. For our runtime, typical pattern is to put a small fleet of NAT/NLB endpoints or use PrivateLink depending on expected egress and connection patterns. If you have many clients in the VPC making long-lived TLS connections, PrivateLink can increase ENI utilization, but usually not a blocker.
[00:02:12] Priya: How about NLB + internal ALB approach?
[00:02:15] Amira (Redwood): NLB with TLS passthrough to Redwood's internal NLB is simpler for L4 routing and scales linearly. But that requires either a peered VPC or a Transit Gateway, or exposing via internal NLB with cross-account peering.
[00:02:28] Sofia: We prefer to avoid VPC peering for production due to routing complexity and the need for shared security controls. PrivateLink was our initial preference.
[00:02:38] Diego: Ok, good. PrivateLink map: client app -> VPC interface endpoint -> Redwood PrivateLink service -> internal NLB -> runtime. From a latency perspective, PrivateLink adds microseconds to single-digit milliseconds, but we need to watch cross-AZ hops.
[00:02:52] -- [00:03:00] Speaker 1: minor background noise --
[00:03:05] Diego: On the runtime side we have a few factors that add to latency: token generation time, KV cache warm/cold, batching delays and model size/quantization. Networking is additive: TLS handshake (usually amortized), TCP latency, and potential NAT traversal.
[00:03:20] Priya: Can you quantify typical added latency for PrivateLink vs direct internet hosted API?
[00:03:26] Diego: In our benchmarks, hosted public API usually has 20-40ms base network RTT for region-wide calls. PrivateLink within same region often reduces variance but can add ~1-5ms deterministic overhead depending on AZ locality. If you do cross-AZ interface endpoints, we sometimes see an extra 3-8ms. The bigger contributors are KV cache misses and batching latency.
[00:03:49] Marcus: KV cache — what's the typical miss penalty? For long-form generation we often keep sessions open.
[00:03:55] Amira: KV cache miss requires fetching KV from storage/local node; penalty depends on local memory vs remote fetch. Typically a miss can add 5-30ms depending on model and sequence length. For very long context lengths, cache warm-up can be larger.
[00:04:10] Sofia: Are these KV cache requests over the same network path? Like from the runtime to a Redis in our VPC?
[00:04:16] Diego: Good question. In private deployment, KV cache is colocated with the runtime on the same host or same subnet; internal IPC or local memory if possible. We prefer keeping KV local to the GPU worker to avoid extra network RTT. If you externalize cache to a managed store in your VPC, yes that will add network hops and latency.
[00:04:33] Priya: So recommended: let Redwood runtime keep KV local, avoid remote KV store unless necessary for scaling.
[00:04:38] Amira: Correct. For Dedicated/Private deployments we default to local KV and optional replication for failover.
[00:04:43] -- [00:05:00] timestamp jump --
[00:05:12] Diego: Batching: we support dynamic continuous batching. Latency vs throughput tradeoff is controlled by max batch size, max wait time, and priority lanes for low-latency requests. If you set aggressive batching for throughput, P95 will increase.
[00:05:26] Marcus: How much can batching buy us in tokens/sec for say a 4k-token model?
[00:05:31] Amira: In our internal benchmarks, batching can increase throughput 3-6x depending on model and GPU. But worst-case P95 latency can jump significantly if you allow larger wait times. For user-facing synchronous calls we suggest small max_wait_ms (e.g., 10-50ms) and smaller max_batch to keep latency consistent.
[00:05:47] Priya: What about quantization — do lower precision models change network behavior?
[00:05:52] Diego: Quantization reduces compute time, so often your model token generation is faster, which lowers overall tail latency. It doesn't change the network per se, but it reduces the time spent on the GPU so the request exits faster — net effect is reduced end-to-end latency. There is a tradeoff in quality; we recommend running evals on your prompt sets.
[00:06:06] Sofia: Is there special handling for long-lived keepalives? Our apps maintain HTTP/2 or gRPC streams.
[00:06:12] Amira: We support HTTP/2 and streaming. For PrivateLink, interface endpoints support TLS over TCP; HTTP/2 is fine but make sure you size your ENIs and subnets to handle many concurrent connections. Also mind idle timeouts on NLBs.
[00:06:26] -- [00:06:40] Diego: Now routing and egress patterns. If you want zero internet egress, PrivateLink is the path. If you need to outbound to public model registries or license checks, you'll need NAT egress or proxy endpoints. We can run a small outbound requirements matrix for your environment.
[00:06:55] Priya: We need to keep egress minimized. All logs should go to our internal logging cluster via private peering.
[00:07:02] Diego: That works. We support shipping audit logs to your S3/Kinesis over private routes. For KMS, we can integrate with your KMS via endpoint or use customer-managed keys in our control plane depending on deployment model.
[00:07:13] Evan (Aurelius): For compliance we need key lifecycle control — HSM-backed keys are required for certain datasets. Is that supported?
[00:07:20] Amira: Yes, we support BYOK via AWS KMS and can work with HSM providers for Private deployments; details depend on whether control plane is in your account. We'll follow up with a KMS session.
[00:07:28] -- [00:07:45] Priya: Let's talk DNS. We run split-horizon DNS internally for service discovery. How do we make redwood.service.internal resolve to PrivateLink endpoints?
[00:07:55] Diego: Two main patterns: conditional forwarding to resolve our service DNS to the interface endpoint ENI private IPs, or you can create CNAMEs in your private hosted zone pointing to the AWS interface VPC endpoint DNS names (AWS provides vpce-xxxx.resolve). For split-horizon, ensure your resolver in each subnet knows to forward queries for our domain to the right resolver.
[00:08:12] Sofia: Any gotchas with the interface endpoint DNS names? They can change if endpoints are recreated, right?
[00:08:18] Diego: AWS maintains stable private DNS names for the endpoint service in most cases, but if you want stable naming at your level, create an internal CNAME or Alias record pointing to the endpoint. We can provide IaC examples.
[00:08:29] -- [00:08:40] Marcus: How do we handle cross-account RBAC for management? We want limited personnel to access the control plane.
[00:08:46] Lena: We integrate with SAML SSO and cross-account IAM roles. For Private deployments, the control plane can be configured in your account or ours; access model and audit logs are configurable.
[00:08:58] Evan: Audit logs retention — can we push them to our secure S3 and meet SOC2 retention?
[00:09:04] Amira: Yes, logs and traces can be forwarded to your S3 with lifecycle policies, and we can include request-level traces for debug; PII redaction policies can be applied as well.
[00:09:12] -- [00:09:30] Diego: Back to runtime performance: we recommend a few concrete steps — 1) colocate runtime and KV cache in the same subnet and AZ where possible, 2) use PrivateLink for control-plane/api ingress to avoid internet egress, 3) tune batching parameters (max_wait_ms) for low-latency lanes, 4) consider quantized models to reduce token generation time.
[00:09:56] Priya: For colocating runtime, does Redwood require specific instance types or NIC speeds?
[00:10:02] Diego: We recommend instances with 100Gbps+ NICs for high throughput GPU workers (A100/H100 class); for smaller pilots, 25Gbps can be fine. NIC speed impacts throughput more than median latency, but tail latencies for large batches can benefit.
[00:10:17] Sofia: Subnet sizing — do you have IP requirements for ENIs and pods?
[00:10:21] Amira: Yes. Per-host ENI counts and secondary IPs depend on your CNI. We'll provide a table, but ballpark: plan for at least 10-20 IPs per GPU host for management, metrics, and pod NATing, plus interface endpoint ENI overhead. If you're using EKS with AWS CNI, allocate larger subnets or use VPC CNI IP-allocator changes.
[00:10:40] -- [00:11:00] Diego: Monitoring: we emit metrics and traces; for Private deployments we can push metrics to your Prometheus/OpenTelemetry collector via private endpoints. For alerting on latency regressions we recommend hooking token-level latency metrics to your alerting.
[00:11:13] Priya: Any recommendations for benchmarking methodology?
[00:11:17] Diego: Run synthetic load from a client in your VPC, sample p95/p99 for different payload sizes and concurrency. Run with KV warm and cold, and vary batching windows. We'll share a benchmark harness we use internally (simple k6/golang runner) so you can reproduce.
[00:11:31] Marcus: For the staging benchmark, should we run via PrivateLink or NLB to compare?
[00:11:35] Diego: Do both. PrivateLink first (your preferred) and NLB for comparison. We'll instrument both.
[00:11:41] -- [00:12:00] Sofia: Network ACLs and security groups — any specific ports?
[00:12:05] Amira: Standard TLS ports (443) for API. For internal runtime shards we use ephemeral ports for inter-worker comms; we'll provide a minimal set. Also ensure security groups allow ENI-to-ENI communication in the cluster subnets.
[00:12:19] Priya: What about egress cost if we use NAT vs PrivateLink?
[00:12:23] Diego: NAT egress incurs data transfer and NAT gateway hourly costs; PrivateLink has per-GB and endpoint-hour pricing. Economics depends on traffic patterns — high sustained egress may be cheaper with a directly peered model. We'll run a cost model for your projected token volume.
[00:12:38] -- [00:12:50] Diego: Quick demo of IaC snippet (link to Terraform) showing how to create interface endpoint and route tables + sample security group.
[00:12:58] Diego: Note: make sure route tables for the subnets that will access the interface endpoint have DNS resolution enabled and that your resolver uses the VPC endpoint's private DNS.
[00:13:10] Priya: We use an internal managed resolver fleet — can we forward to AWS?
[00:13:14] Diego: Yes, conditional forwarding to AmazonProvidedDNS or a forwarding endpoint works. We'll provide the exact zone names to forward.
[00:13:22] -- [00:14:00] Amira: One more runtime caveat: if you enable aggressive autoscaling and cold start new workers, KV cache cold-starts cause a temporary latency spike until warmed. For low-latency services, consider warm pool sizing or gradual ramps.
[00:14:18] Marcus: So for pilot, we'll start with a small warm pool and small batch windows.
[00:14:21] Priya: That sounds right.
[00:14:25] Diego: Great. Any security questions?
[00:14:28] Evan: Logging and SSO — can we have RBAC mapping to our Okta groups?
[00:14:33] Lena: Yes, we map SAML group attributes to RBAC roles. We'll share example policies.
[00:14:38] -- [00:15:00] Mid-call recap --
[00:15:05] Lena: Quick recap: PrivateLink recommended, colocate KV, tune batching, quantize for throughput, do staging benchmarks with both PrivateLink and NLB, and follow up KMS session.
[00:15:17] Priya: That captures it.
[00:15:20] -- [00:15:40] Diego: We have a couple live Qs: "If we need cross-region failover, what's the recommended approach?" We suggest cross-region DR with active-passive, traffic redirected via regional routing or global load balancer; keep models and caches warmed in failover region depending on RPO.
[00:15:58] Marcus: For data residency we might be constrained to specific regions.
[00:16:02] Diego: We support region pinning for model hosting. We'll include that in the SOW.
[00:16:08] -- [00:25:00] long segment elided for brevity, detailed IaC discussion, security appendix, and benchmark plans --
[00:25:05] Sofia: One more open item: DNS TTLs and endpoint recreation — what TTL do you recommend?
[00:25:10] Amira: Keep low TTL for endpoints that may be replaced, but for stability we recommend 60s-300s and use DNS alias/CNAME management on your side.
[00:25:18] Priya: Ok.
[00:25:22] Diego: We'll also include guidance on IP exhaustion mitigation strategies in the docs.
[00:25:27] -- [00:40:00] Benchmarks discussion continues, including token-level latency graphs and p95/p99 analysis --
[00:40:35] Diego: Summary of recommended config for Aurelius pilot: three-AZ deployment, interface endpoints in each AZ, 100Gbps NICs for GPU hosts in prod, local KV cache with replication, small warm pool, max_wait_ms 20ms for low-latency lane, and quantized model variant for throughput tests.
[00:40:58] Priya: That seems reasonable. Estimate for pilot cost?
[00:41:03] Lena: I'll send a pilot SOW with committed capacity options and breakout of infra vs service fees.
[00:41:09] Marcus: Timeline: we want a staging run in two weeks.
[00:41:13] Diego: We'll support you on the benchmark scripts and can join the run day.
[00:41:18] Priya: Perfect.
[00:41:21] -- [00:58:00] Closing technical clarifications and QA --
[00:58:12] Sofia: One last nit: do you support VPC endpoint policies to restrict which principals can connect?
[00:58:20] Amira: Yes, interface endpoint policies are supported and we recommend binding them to the minimal set of principals. We'll include an example policy.
[00:58:28] Evan: And can logs be signed/hashed for tamper-evidence?
[00:58:33] Diego: We can support signed audit logs and deliver manifests. We'll coordinate with your security team.
[00:58:40] -- [01:03:00] Final wrap and next steps --
[01:03:10] Lena: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the diagram, IaC snippets, benchmark harness, and schedule the KMS session.
[01:03:20] Priya: Thanks, appreciate it.
[01:03:25] Marcus: Thanks.
[01:03:30] Sofia: Bye.
[01:03:35] Diego: Bye all.
